course_name_original: COMPLEMENTI DI SISTEMI OPERATIVI Canale unico
course_name_en: COMPLEMENTS OF OPERATING SYSTEMS Single channel
prerequisites: Knowledge of basic algorithms and data structures - lists/trees/associative maps
Knowledge of C language and CPU
Knowledge of the machine model (Von Neumann) and rudiments of assembly
Familiarity with the Linux operating system and its tools

learning_outcomes.text: Know the structure of an operating system, and frame the historical perspective that led to current choices. The course alternates practice and theory. Each concept presented in class is supported by a 'practical' lesson that typically consists of developing one or more programs. The practical sessions involve intervals between problem presentation and solution presentation, during which students are invited to propose their own.

Structure of an operating system and mechanisms for managing its functionalities. Learn the functioning of basic mechanisms that implement critical operating system functionalities (context switch, system calls, memory management, file systems).
Experience the functioning of these mechanisms by developing them in 'sandboxed' environments and on bare-metal systems.
Learn basic concepts for interacting with the kernel of an operating system when opening devices (cameras, serials, joysticks).

Be able to design bare metal applications that incorporate operating system functionalities. Be able to interact with an operating system at a low level. Be able to understand and configure various aspects of such a system.

Characterization of the performance of various subsystems. Experience, through the proposed and developed programs, concrete effects that implementative and design choices have on the performance of these subsystems.

The course includes numerous exercises to be carried out preferably in groups and shared on network version management platforms (git). The experience of interaction through these platforms aims to prepare future engineers for the use of tools and the understanding of communicative dynamics typical in a development team. In addition, the course includes, as an integral part of the exam, the presentation of a project consisting of the design and development of a program and the writing of its related documentation.
Presentation of an 'in-depth' vision of a computer system. Emphasis on 'open-box' observation, in which students are invited to think about how the tools they use work, rather than just using them.
knowledge of the role of the operating system in modern computing systems

knowledge of the algorithms and data structures underlying the operating system kernel (with practical references). These include: context switch, memory allocation, virtual memory management (MMU management), knowledge of CPU and disk scheduling algorithms and systems, characterization of operating system subsystem performance.
The ultimate goal is to provide the student with the tools to understand what happens at the hardware level whenever high-level operations are requested from the machine.

syllabus_topics: Complements of C programming for Operating Systems
Example of bare metal programming on microcontroller
Development of interrupt handler on microcontroller
Creation of a preemptive scheduler in user space
FIFO, SJF, SRJF, Round Robin, Round Robin with Priority
assessment_rules: The exam consists of a written test AND a project presentation. The written test involves 8 exercises to be completed in approximately one and a half hours. The project consists of creating a program agreed upon with the lecturer and must be done in C/C++. Group work is allowed for the project, and individual contributions will be tracked using versioning systems.
